criteria_results.title: Title VII damages instruction does NOT disclose the $200,000 statutory cap to the jury
criteria_results.reasoning: The actual proposed jury instructions and special verdict form instruct on compensatory and punitive damages without stating any specific Title VII damages cap. Although a drafting note references the $200,000 cap and says not to mention it to the jury, that note is not part of the jury-facing instruction and the instructions themselves do not disclose a statutory ceiling.

criteria_results.title: Cover memo explains that Title VII damages cap is not disclosed to jury
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memo expressly addresses the Title VII statutory damages cap, identifies the applicable $200,000 cap under 42 U.S.C. § 1981a(b)(3), and states that the jury may not be told about it, with the verdict form structured to protect application of the cap. Although it does not use the exact phrase that the court applies the cap post-verdict, it sufficiently discusses the nondisclosure issue contemplated by the criterion.

criteria_results.title: No Faragher/Ellerth instruction included for the retaliation claim
criteria_results.reasoning: The proposed instructions expressly state that Defendant does not propose a Faragher/Ellerth affirmative defense instruction, and no such defense instruction is included for the Title VII retaliation claim.

criteria_results.title: Cover memo identifies defendant's Faragher/Ellerth request for retaliation claim
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memo explicitly identifies Brief No. 2 as a Faragher/Ellerth instruction request, states it concerned the retaliation claim, and recommends withdrawing it because the order says the defense has no application to Title VII retaliation.

criteria_results.title: Cover memo explains legal basis for excluding Faragher/Ellerth from retaliation
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memo states that Faragher/Ellerth has no application to the Title VII retaliation claim and explains that the defense applies to supervisor harassment where no tangible employment action was taken, whereas this case involves termination/retaliation. Although it does not use the exact phrase “vicarious liability,” it sufficiently explains the relevant legal distinction for excluding the instruction.

criteria_results.title: Title VII retaliation instruction uses but-for causation standard
criteria_results.reasoning: The Title VII retaliation instructions expressly require Plaintiff to prove that her January 17, 2023 protected activity was the “but-for” cause of Creston’s termination decision, state that motivating-factor or contributing-factor causation is insufficient, and distinguish this standard from the Ohio Whistleblower contributing-factor standard. This is consistent with Nassar.

criteria_results.title: Ohio Whistleblower instruction uses contributing-factor causation standard
criteria_results.reasoning: The Ohio Whistleblower instructions expressly require Plaintiff to prove that the Ohio EPA report was a “contributing factor” in the termination, define that as actually playing a part in the decision, and state that this standard is different from and less demanding than the Title VII but-for standard. The special verdict form also uses contributing-factor causation for the Ohio Whistleblower claim.

criteria_results.title: Cover memo explains different causation standards for the two retaliation claims
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memo does discuss different causation standards: Title VII retaliation uses a but-for standard and the Ohio Whistleblower claim uses a contributing-factor standard. However, the criterion specifically requires the memo to cite or reference Nassar for the Title VII but-for causation standard, and the memo does not mention Nassar.

criteria_results.title: Cover memo identifies plaintiff's mixed-motive request as legally incorrect
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memo discusses but-for causation for Title VII retaliation and contrasting standards, but it does not identify that plaintiff's pretrial brief requested a mixed-motive instruction, nor does it explain that such an instruction is legally incorrect under Nassar because Title VII retaliation requires but-for causation.

criteria_results.title: After-acquired evidence instruction is included
criteria_results.reasoning: The proposed jury instructions include Defendant’s Proposed Instruction No. 14 titled “After-Acquired Evidence,” specifically addressing Okafor-Reyes’s alleged MBA misrepresentation on her 2016 employment application and its effect on damages.

criteria_results.title: After-acquired evidence instruction frames doctrine as remedies limitation, not complete defense
criteria_results.reasoning: Instruction No. 14 expressly states that after-acquired evidence “is not a defense to liability on any of Plaintiff’s claims” and may only “limit the lost wages and benefits Plaintiff may recover,” cutting off recovery after the discovery date if proven. This tracks McKennon as a remedies limitation rather than a complete defense.

criteria_results.title: Cover memo explains after-acquired evidence is remedies limitation per McKennon
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memo explicitly states that McKennon holds after-acquired evidence does not bar liability and is not a complete defense, but instead limits remedies such as reinstatement/front pay and cuts off back pay as of the discovery date if the employer proves it would have terminated the employee.

criteria_results.title: Cover memo notes defendant's overbroad framing of after-acquired evidence as complete defense
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memo explicitly notes that the pretrial brief framed after-acquired evidence as a "complete defense to all claims" and explains that this is legally incorrect under McKennon because it limits remedies rather than barring liability.

criteria_results.title: Ohio Whistleblower instruction addresses internal-reporting prerequisite under ORC § 4113.52
criteria_results.reasoning: The Ohio Whistleblower instructions expressly include the internal-reporting prerequisite. Instruction No. 7 requires the jury to decide whether Plaintiff complied with the internal-reporting requirements before considering the claim, and Instruction No. 8 details that she must have orally notified a supervisor/responsible officer, filed a written report, and allowed Creston an opportunity to correct or make a good-faith correction effort before the external Ohio EPA report. The verdict form also asks the jury to make this finding.

criteria_results.title: Internal-reporting instruction treats verbal report as disputed factual issue for jury
criteria_results.reasoning: Instruction No. 8 expressly states that Plaintiff contends she orally reported to Plant Manager Greg Felton on February 28, 2023, that Creston disputes any such report, and that it is for the jury to decide whether Plaintiff proved the oral notification. It does not assume the report occurred or did not occur.

criteria_results.title: Implied-contract instruction references at-will disclaimer from Employee Handbook
criteria_results.reasoning: The breach of implied employment contract instruction (Proposed Instruction No. 10) expressly references the Employee Handbook’s page 3 at-will provision, including that nothing in the handbook creates a contract of employment and that employment may be terminated at any time for any lawful reason.

criteria_results.title: Implied-contract instruction references progressive-discipline provision from Employee Handbook
criteria_results.reasoning: The breach of implied employment contract instruction expressly states that the claim is based on Creston allegedly failing to follow the progressive-discipline procedure on pages 27 and 28 of the Employee Handbook, and repeatedly references whether that progressive-discipline provision was binding and applicable.

criteria_results.title: Implied-contract instruction presents conflict between disclaimer and progressive discipline for jury determination
criteria_results.reasoning: The breach-of-implied-contract instruction expressly tells the jury to decide whether Creston and Plaintiff mutually intended the handbook’s progressive-discipline provision to be a binding term despite the at-will disclaimer. It directs jurors to consider the handbook as a whole, including the disclaimer, reservation-of-rights language, progressive-discipline language, and reliance. The special verdict form likewise asks the jury to resolve whether the provision became a binding limitation on termination. Thus, it presents the disclaimer/progressive-discipline tension as a factual question rather than resolving it as a matter of law.

criteria_results.title: Implied-contract instruction reflects Ohio law (Mers v. Dispatch Printing Co.)
criteria_results.reasoning: The implied-contract instruction expressly cites Mers v. Dispatch Printing Co. and related Ohio cases, recognizes that handbook provisions may become binding implied contract terms if mutual intent and other circumstances support that result, and treats at-will disclaimers as factors rather than as automatically dispositive. It therefore reflects Ohio law under Mers rather than incorrectly stating that disclaimers always defeat implied contract claims.

criteria_results.title: Mitigation instruction is included
criteria_results.reasoning: The instruction set includes a specific failure-to-mitigate damages instruction: Proposed Instruction No. 13, titled “Mitigation of Damages,” which explains Plaintiff’s duty to mitigate, Defendant’s burden, substantially equivalent employment, and reduction of lost wages. The special verdict form also includes mitigation questions.

criteria_results.title: Mitigation instruction places burden of proof on defendant
criteria_results.reasoning: The mitigation instruction expressly states that Creston/Defendant bears the burden of proving by a preponderance of the evidence that Plaintiff failed to mitigate her damages, and the verdict form is consistent with that allocation.

criteria_results.title: Cover memo notes correction of mitigation burden from defendant's brief
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memo expressly states that Brief No. 4 improperly places the mitigation burden on Plaintiff, explains that under Sixth Circuit law the employer/defendant bears the burden of proving failure to mitigate, and cites Rasimas and Ford Motor Co. v. EEOC as authority.

criteria_results.title: Temporal proximity / circumstantial evidence instruction included for retaliation
criteria_results.reasoning: The proposed instructions include a specific “Timing of Events” instruction telling jurors they may consider the timing and length of time between protected activity and adverse action as circumstantial evidence of causation, and that timing must be weighed with all other evidence. The instructions also identify the relevant protected-activity and termination dates, and drafting notes account for Exhibit 14/Cavender as bridging the temporal gap. Although the instruction does not expressly spell out “13 days” and “approximately 5 months,” it provides guidance on temporal proximity as circumstantial evidence of retaliation.

criteria_results.title: Temporal proximity instruction permits inference of retaliatory motive
criteria_results.reasoning: The temporal proximity instruction expressly allows the jury to consider the timing of events and states that a short interval between protected activity and adverse action may, together with other evidence, support an inference of causation/retaliatory motive. It does not direct the jury to disregard temporal proximity entirely.

criteria_results.title: Temporal proximity instruction does not mandate finding of retaliation
criteria_results.reasoning: The temporal proximity instruction states that timing is only one circumstance to be weighed with all evidence and expressly says that an adverse action following protected activity does not, by itself, prove causation. It does not direct the jury that temporal proximity alone conclusively establishes retaliation.

criteria_results.title: Kolstad good-faith defense instruction included for punitive damages
criteria_results.reasoning: The proposed instructions include a punitive damages instruction for the Title VII claim that expressly incorporates the Kolstad good-faith defense, stating that punitive damages may not be awarded if Creston proves it made good-faith efforts to comply with Title VII and the managerial employee’s conduct was contrary to those efforts. It also cites Kolstad as authority.

criteria_results.title: Kolstad defense is distinguished from Faragher/Ellerth in the instructions or memo
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly distinguishes the doctrines: it recommends withdrawing the Faragher/Ellerth instruction because that defense applies to supervisor harassment/vicarious liability and not Title VII retaliation, while explaining that the same policy/training evidence should instead be used for the Kolstad good-faith defense to punitive damages. It also separately discusses Kolstad as a punitive-damages defense requiring implementation of anti-discrimination policies.

criteria_results.title: Special verdict form (not general verdict) is included
criteria_results.reasoning: The output includes a section titled “DEFENDANT'S PROPOSED SPECIAL VERDICT FORM” with multiple specific interrogatories/questions organized by claim, including liability, causation, damages, mitigation, after-acquired evidence, and punitive damages questions. This is a special verdict form, not merely a general verdict form.

criteria_results.title: Special verdict form has separate interrogatories for Title VII retaliation claim
criteria_results.reasoning: The proposed special verdict form contains a dedicated section labeled “PART I — COUNT I: TITLE VII RETALIATION,” with separate questions addressing causation, damages, punitive damages, and the good-faith defense for that claim.

criteria_results.title: Special verdict form has separate interrogatories for Ohio Whistleblower claim
criteria_results.reasoning: The proposed special verdict form contains a distinct Part II labeled “COUNT II: OHIO WHISTLEBLOWER PROTECTION ACT,” with separate questions addressing internal reporting compliance, contributing-factor causation, damages, mitigation, and after-acquired evidence for that claim.

criteria_results.title: Special verdict form has separate interrogatories for implied employment contract claim
criteria_results.reasoning: The proposed special verdict form includes a distinct Part III titled “COUNT IV: BREACH OF IMPLIED CONTRACT,” with separate Questions 13–15 addressing mutual intent, applicability of the progressive-discipline provision, and damages for the implied employment contract claim.

criteria_results.title: Title VII retaliation damages instruction includes compensatory and punitive damages
criteria_results.reasoning: The damages instructions expressly address compensatory damages for the Title VII claim, including emotional distress and related medical expenses in Instruction No. 15, and punitive damages for the Title VII claim in Instruction No. 16. The special verdict form also includes emotional distress damages and punitive damages for the Title VII retaliation claim.

criteria_results.title: Ohio Whistleblower damages instruction is differentiated from Title VII damages
criteria_results.reasoning: The output separates damages by claim in the verdict form and expressly instructs that punitive damages are available only for the Title VII claim, not the Ohio Whistleblower claim or contract claim. It also flags emotional-distress damages for the Ohio Whistleblower claim as bracketed/subject to confirmation rather than automatically treating them identically to Title VII damages.

criteria_results.title: Implied-contract damages instruction reflects contract damages measure
criteria_results.reasoning: The instructions expressly state that emotional distress and punitive damages are not recoverable on the breach-of-contract claim. The Title VII/whistleblower damages categories are not applied to the implied-contract claim, and the verdict form asks only for economic damages caused by the failure to follow the progressive-discipline provision, which reflects a contract-style damages measure rather than tort/statutory damages.

criteria_results.title: Pre-existing condition / eggshell plaintiff instruction included for emotional distress
criteria_results.reasoning: The proposed instructions include Instruction No. 15 on compensatory damages for emotional distress, expressly referencing Plaintiff’s pre-existing anxiety condition treated beginning in 2020. It explains that Plaintiff cannot recover for the pre-existing condition itself, may recover only for aggravation caused by Creston’s unlawful conduct, and includes eggshell-plaintiff language that Creston is liable for the full extent of any caused aggravation even if Plaintiff was more susceptible to harm.

criteria_results.title: Preliminary instructions on role of jury included
criteria_results.reasoning: The output does not include a drafted preliminary instruction explaining the jury’s role and duties, such as deciding facts and following the court’s law. It only requests that the Court give customary general instructions on duties of the jury, which is not itself an included instruction.

criteria_results.title: Preliminary instruction on burden of proof included
criteria_results.reasoning: The instruction set includes Proposed Instruction No. 1, titled “Burden of Proof — Preponderance of the Evidence,” which expressly states that Plaintiff bears the burden of proving each element of each claim by a preponderance of the evidence and defines that standard.

criteria_results.title: Standard witness credibility instruction included
criteria_results.reasoning: The proposed instructions do not include an actual standard witness credibility instruction advising jurors to consider factors such as demeanor, bias, interest, consistency, or corroboration. The output merely requests the Court's customary general instructions and references credibility generally, which does not satisfy the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Title VII retaliation elements instruction included
criteria_results.reasoning: The instruction set includes a substantive Title VII retaliation elements instruction (Proposed Instruction No. 2) listing protected activity, materially adverse action, and but-for causation between the protected activity and termination.

criteria_results.title: Ohio Whistleblower elements instruction included
criteria_results.reasoning: The instruction set includes a substantive Ohio Whistleblower Protection Act elements instruction in Proposed Instruction No. 7, identifying the internal-reporting prerequisite, adverse employment action, and contributing-factor causation based on Plaintiff’s March 9, 2023 Ohio EPA report. Proposed Instruction No. 8 further details the internal-reporting requirements. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Implied employment contract elements instruction included
criteria_results.reasoning: The instruction set includes a substantive implied employment contract instruction in Proposed Instruction No. 10. It sets out elements requiring the jury to decide whether the handbook’s progressive-discipline provision became a binding contractual term limiting termination, whether it applied to plaintiff’s termination/RIF, and whether Creston failed to comply causing damages. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Legitimate non-retaliatory reason (RIF) instruction included
criteria_results.reasoning: The proposed instructions include Instruction No. 5, titled “Legitimate Business Reason; Reduction in Force; Business Judgment,” which expressly states that Creston contends it terminated Plaintiff because her position was eliminated in a company-wide RIF for financial reasons. It also instructs the jury to consider whether Creston’s stated reason is believable and that, if the stated reason is not the true reason, the jury may infer retaliation. This adequately addresses the legitimate non-retaliatory reason and pretext framework.

criteria_results.title: Protected activity instruction uses reasonable good-faith belief standard
criteria_results.reasoning: The Title VII instruction does not require the jury to find that actual pay discrimination occurred. Instead, it tells the jury that the court has already determined Plaintiff’s January 17, 2023 internal complaint was protected activity and that the jury should treat that element as established. Although it does not expressly state the reasonable, good-faith belief standard, it avoids the prohibited actual-discrimination requirement and makes protected activity not an issue for the jury.

criteria_results.title: Citations to Sixth Circuit Pattern Jury Instructions included
criteria_results.reasoning: The document expressly states that the Sixth Circuit has not promulgated pattern civil jury instructions and cites cases, OJI-CV, Seventh Circuit, and Eleventh Circuit pattern instructions, but it does not cite any Sixth Circuit Pattern Jury Instructions (Civil) or specific Sixth Circuit pattern instruction numbers/titles anywhere.

criteria_results.title: Cover memo lists each instruction with its legal basis
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo identifies many proposed instructions and discusses legal authorities for several (e.g., McKennon, Rasimas, R.C. 4113.52, Mickey, Staub, Mers, Kolstad). But it does not list each proposed instruction Nos. 1–16 and pair each with a specific legal basis. Several instructions or groups, such as business judgment/pretext, general damages/no double recovery, back pay, and some limiting/damages instructions, are mentioned without specific statutes, cases, or pattern instruction numbers. The memo also states that pattern-instruction numbers and citations remain to be verified rather than providing them.

criteria_results.title: Cover memo identifies rejected instruction requests with reasoning
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memo identifies multiple instruction requests that should be withdrawn, replaced, or would be refused, and provides legal reasoning for each. For example, it recommends withdrawing the Faragher/Ellerth instruction because the court said the defense has no application to retaliation and would not entertain it; it rejects the after-acquired evidence instruction as a complete defense because McKennon limits it to remedies, not liability; and it rejects/replaces the mitigation instruction because Sixth Circuit law places the burden on the employer. This satisfies the requirement to identify at least two rejected instruction requests with reasoning.

criteria_results.title: Cover memo identifies areas requiring particular legal care
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memo clearly identifies numerous specific legal issues requiring careful drafting, including differing causation standards for Title VII and Ohio WPA claims, the Kolstad punitive-damages defense versus Faragher/Ellerth, after-acquired evidence under McKennon, mitigation burden under Rasimas/Ford, the Title VII damages cap, and Mers implied-contract analysis. This exceeds the requirement of at least two named areas of legal complexity.

criteria_results.title: Instructions organized by claim as required by standing order
criteria_results.reasoning: The proposed instructions are clearly structured with claim-specific headings and sections: Count I Title VII retaliation (Instructions 2–4), Count II Ohio Whistleblower (Instructions 7–9), and Count IV implied contract (Instruction 10), along with general and damages instructions. The special verdict form is also organized by claim. Although some instructions address overlapping issues for multiple claims, the overall structure is not an undifferentiated mass and satisfies the claim-by-claim organization requirement.

criteria_results.title: Punitive damages instruction included for Title VII claim
criteria_results.reasoning: The instruction set includes Defendant's Proposed Instruction No. 16 titled “Punitive Damages — Title VII Claim Only; Good-Faith Compliance.” It expressly states punitive damages may be considered only on the Title VII claim and explains the standard requiring proof that a managerial employee acted with malice or reckless indifference to federally protected rights, along with the Kolstad good-faith compliance defense.

criteria_results.title: Special verdict form includes separate damages questions per claim
criteria_results.reasoning: The special verdict form asks for damages separately by claim: Question 2 for Title VII retaliation, Question 10 for the Ohio Whistleblower claim, and Question 15 for the implied contract claim. It does not use a single combined damages figure across all claims.

criteria_results.title: Mitigation instruction references case-specific factual considerations
criteria_results.reasoning: The output includes a mitigation instruction and, in the mitigation section’s drafting note, references case-specific facts: the December 2023 Archer-Lawson job offer, its $89,000 salary compared to Plaintiff’s $97,200 Creston salary, comparable account-management duties, Cleveland area, and the August–November 2023 job-search gap. Thus it is not purely abstract.

criteria_results.title: Proposed jury instructions document produced
criteria_results.reasoning: The agent produced a document labeled proposed-jury-instructions.docx containing numerous proposed jury instructions and a proposed special verdict form. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Cover memorandum produced as separate deliverable
criteria_results.reasoning: The agent produced a distinct separate deliverable titled “instruction-cover-memo.docx,” with memorandum formatting and content separate from the proposed jury instructions document.

criteria_results.title: Instructions advance at least two identifiable defense positions
criteria_results.reasoning: The proposed instructions incorporate multiple identifiable defense-favorable positions, including the Title VII but-for causation standard, the RIF/business-judgment rationale as a legitimate non-retaliatory reason, the Ohio Whistleblower internal-reporting prerequisite, mitigation, after-acquired evidence limiting damages, and the Kolstad good-faith defense to punitive damages. These positions are presented in generally legally accurate form for purposes of the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Emotional distress / compensatory damages instruction included
criteria_results.reasoning: The instruction set includes Proposed Instruction No. 15, titled “Compensatory Damages — Emotional Distress; Pre-Existing Condition,” which applies at least to the Title VII claim and explains what the jury may consider in awarding emotional distress damages, including pain, suffering, inconvenience, mental anguish, medical expenses, causation, pre-existing conditions, and limits on recovery.

criteria_results.title: Back pay instruction included
criteria_results.reasoning: The instruction set includes Proposed Instruction No. 12 titled “Lost Wages and Benefits (Back Pay),” which explains that the jury may award wages and benefits from termination through verdict, less amounts earned from other employment, and gives guidance on included compensation and future earnings.

criteria_results.title: No hostile-work-environment instruction included (claim was dismissed)
criteria_results.reasoning: The proposed jury instructions identify that the hostile-work-environment claim was dismissed and do not include any substantive instruction for a hostile-work-environment claim. The only references are limiting/background statements noting dismissal or excluding damages based on dismissed claims.
